title: Uruguay and Brazil
subtitle: South America's Atlantic side
objectives: Compare them with the Andean countries

steps.title: Uruguay
steps.body: Uruguay has a humid, maritime climate influenced by the Atlantic and the Río de la Plata. Tannat, brought by Basque immigrants in the 1870s, is its national grape, giving dark, tannic reds that are often softer than in France's Madiran. Canelones, near Montevideo, is the main region; Maldonado, on the coast, makes fresh whites like Albariño.

steps.title: Brazil
steps.body: Brazil's main region is Serra Gaúcha, in the far south, settled by Italian immigrants. It's wet and humid, which suits early-picked grapes for sparkling wine, now Brazil's strength. Vale dos Vinhedos was its first GI. In the north-east, the São Francisco Valley, near the equator, harvests twice a year with irrigation.

steps.prompt: Why is sparkling wine well suited to Serra Gaúcha?
options: Its humid climate suits early-picked, high-acid grapes
It has very hot, dry summers
steps.explanation: Rain and humidity make full ripeness hard; early picking for sparkling wine keeps acidity and avoids rot.

steps.title: Different from the Andes
steps.body: Unlike Chile and Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil have rain in the growing season, more like Bordeaux than Mendoza. Growers fight disease rather than drought. Their wines tend to be lower in alcohol and fresher, a counterpoint to the ripe, sunny Andean style.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Uruguay's humid climate gives Tannat a softer style
Brazil's strength is sparkling wine from Serra Gaúcha
The Atlantic side fights rain, not drought
